text: Webflow Cloud is a good fit when the app is part of a Webflow managed site
and you want to deploy it alongside that site with minimal hosting and domain setup.
Think interactive tools, campaign experiences, customer portals,
or small web apps that complement Webflow pages.
Choose it when your team already builds and manages the site in Webflow.
The app fits the frameworks and runtime Webflow Cloud currently supports.
As an example, here we used Next.js.
You value one workflow for the Webflow site and its app more than fine-grained control over
infrastructure. And the app's traffic, runtime needs, and operational requirements are within
the platform's limits. Consider alternatives when you need broad framework or back-end flexibility,
custom networking, workers, databases, or control over the infrastructure.
A cloud platform such as AWS, Google Cloud, or Azure is usually a better fit.
You want a general-purpose web app deployment workflow or deeper control over builds and runtime.
Vercel, Netlify, or Cloudflare may fit better depending on the stack.
The app is primarily a product rather than an extension of a Webflow site.
Separating the app's hosting from the marketing site can make architecture and future migrations
simpler. A practical rule. Use Webflow Cloud for a Webflow adjacent app whose requirements
match its supported stack. Choose a general hosting platform when the app's infrastructure
needs should drive the decision. Be sure to check current framework support, limits,
pricing, and deployment features before committing, since those details can change.

This sequence diagram follows the calculator app from source code to a working app in the
visitor's browser. First, the developer pushes the calculator's source code to a GitHub repo and
branch. Then, Webflow Cloud builds the calculator app, a next JS application, and deploys its runtime.
In Webflow Cloud, the normal trigger is a git push to the GitHub branch connected to
the Webflow Cloud environment. Once the app is deployed, the visitor opens the website.
Their browser requests the home page, and the Webflow site returns a landing page
containing a link to the calculator. When the visitor follows that link, the browser requests
slash calculator on the same domain. The Webflow site routes that request to the
calculator application hosted in Webflow Cloud. Webflow Cloud returns the calculator's HTML,
the initial page structure, to the browser. Next, the browser requests the application's
supporting files from the calculator path. These include the JavaScript and styles needed
to make the calculator work and display correctly. Webflow Cloud sends those files back. With the
page structure, JavaScript, and styles loaded, the browser renders the interactive calculator.
The visitor has moved from the Webflow landing page into the Webflow Cloud hosted application
